clips.title: Why computers count 1, 10, 11
clips.body_markdown:
Binary is place value with only two digits. In base 10 each column is worth 10x the one to its right; in base 2 each column is worth 2x: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

So `1011` in binary = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11**.

Hexadecimal (base 16) exists for humans, not machines: one hex digit encodes exactly four bits, so `0xFF` = `11111111` = 255. Two digits, one byte — that's why you see hex everywhere in memory dumps and colors.

clips.title: How a byte becomes a letter
clips.body_markdown:
An unsigned 8-bit byte holds 0–255. Characters are an agreed mapping on top: ASCII says 65 = 'A', 97 = 'a'. Unicode assigns *code points* (e.g. U+0041), and UTF-8 is the storage scheme — it uses 1 byte for ASCII and up to 4 for the rest.

Signed integers use two's complement: the top bit's value is negative, so `1111` in 4-bit signed = -8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = **-1**. One addition circuit handles both + and −. That single design choice is why `char` and `int` are just differently-sized bit buckets.

clips.title: A variable is a named box, a type is the box's shape
clips.body_markdown:
A variable binds a *name* to a *value* stored somewhere in memory. The type tells the language two things: how to interpret the bits, and which operations are legal.

```python
age = 27        # int: numeric bits
name = "Ada"   # str: sequence of chars
```

Statically typed languages check shapes before running; dynamically typed languages check while running. Same boxes, different enforcement time. Most beginner bugs are shape mismatches: adding `"3" + 4` fails not because the values are wrong but because the boxes are.

clips.title: Loops are just conditionals that jump backwards
clips.body_markdown:
Every loop reduces to three parts: an initialization, a condition, and a step that changes something the condition checks.

```python
i = 0            # init
while i < 3:     # condition
    print(i)
    i += 1       # step
```

Forget the step and the condition never becomes false — the classic infinite loop. `for` loops bundle the three parts into one line; `while` keeps them visible. If you can write the init/condition/step triple by hand, no loop syntax in any language will surprise you.

clips.title: Functions: name an algorithm, hide its variables
clips.body_markdown:
A function packages a computation behind a name, takes inputs (parameters), and returns an output. The decisive property is *scope*: variables created inside the function don't exist outside it.

```python
def double(n):
    result = n * 2
    return result

x = double(4)   # 8
# result is gone here
```

That hiding is why functions compose: `double(double(4))` works regardless of the internals. Scope is also the source of classic bugs — reaching for a global instead of passing a parameter couples the function to the outside world.

clips.title: Big-O asks: how does work grow when input grows?
clips.body_markdown:
Big-O ignores constants and machine speed; it describes the *shape* of growth as input size n grows.

- O(1): same work regardless of n — array index lookup
- O(log n): doubling n adds one step — binary search
- O(n): double the input, double the work — one loop
- O(n²): nested loops over the input — compare every pair

```python
for x in items:        # O(n)
    for y in items:    # O(n) again → O(n²)
        compare(x, y)
```

The peephole rule: count how many times you touch the input. Sequential touches multiply, nested touches do too.
